secondary_tickers: INFY.NS / INFY.BO (NSE/BSE, primary listing in India, 1 ADS = 1 equity share)
sector: Information Technology - IT Services and Consulting (India)
overview: Infosys is India's second-largest IT services and consulting company, providing digital transformation, cloud, consulting, business process management (BPM), and AI-first technology services to large global enterprises across financial services, manufacturing, retail, communications, energy/utilities, hi-tech, and life sciences industries. The company operates a global delivery model combining low-cost offshore centers in India with onsite client-facing teams across more than 59-63 countries, and reported FY2026 (fiscal year ended March 31, 2026) revenue of $20.16 billion. It trades as an ADR on the NYSE (CIK 0001067491, 20-F foreign private issuer, March fiscal year end) and on the NSE/BSE in India, with roughly 325,000 employees worldwide.

business_model.summary: Infosys earns revenue primarily through time-and-materials and fixed-price IT services contracts — application development/maintenance, infrastructure management, consulting, digital/cloud engineering, and AI services — supplemented by business process management (BPM, via Infosys BPM) and proprietary software/platforms (Finacle core banking platform, Infosys Topaz AI platform, Infosys Cobalt cloud platform). The bulk of revenue is project-based and transactional rather than subscription-like, though large multi-year outsourcing and managed-services deals (several billion dollars in TCV each quarter) provide multi-year revenue visibility once signed. Delivery is organized around a global onsite-offshore model: a smaller, higher-cost onsite workforce manages client relationships and requirements in North America/Europe while the large offshore workforce in India (and increasingly nearshore/delivery hubs elsewhere) performs the bulk of execution at lower cost, which is the central economic engine of the Indian IT services industry.

revenue_streams.name: Hi-Tech

revenue_streams.name: Life Sciences

business_model.customer_type: Almost entirely B2B/enterprise — large multinational corporations and government/institutional clients across 59-63 countries; client concentration risk exists at the largest-account level though no single client is typically disclosed as exceeding low-single-digit percent of revenue
business_model.geographic_mix: North America ~56%, Europe ~32%, Rest of World ~9%, India ~3% (FY2026); heavy dependence on US and European corporate IT budgets, with the US dollar as the functional reporting currency despite the large majority of costs (employee compensation) being INR-denominated
business_model.unit_economics: Operating margin guided at 20-22% for FY2027 (FY2026 reported IFRS operating margin 20.3%, adjusted non-IFRS 21.0%); utilization (ex-trainees) around 83% in Q4 FY2026; voluntary attrition (LTM, IT services) around 12.6%, indicating a tight but not overheated labor market versus pandemic-era peaks above 25%; free cash flow conversion has been strong, running 90-116% of net profit across recent quarters, supporting the company's capital return policy of returning ~85% of cumulative 5-year free cash flow via dividends and buybacks.

competitive_position.market_position: Second-largest Indian IT services firm by revenue behind TCS, and generally ranked among the top-five global IT services/consulting brands by scale; Accenture remains the clear global leader (~$69.7B FY2025 revenue) with Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech, and Cognizant forming the next competitive tier of large-scale offshore-centric IT services providers.
competitive_position.market_share: Infosys brand valued at ~$16.4 billion (2026, Brand Finance), ranked third among IT services brands behind Accenture (~$42.3B) and TCS (~$21.2B); ~325,000 employees versus TCS's ~607,000, Cognizant's ~336,000, Wipro's ~234,000, and HCLTech's ~220,000 — Infosys recently cited as among the fastest-growing IT services brands globally despite modest headline revenue growth (~3% in constant currency for FY2026)

moat_factors.description: Decades of investment in offshore delivery centers, training infrastructure (its Mysuru campus is one of the world's largest corporate training facilities), and a workforce of ~325,000 create a cost and capacity barrier difficult for smaller or newer entrants to replicate at scale

moat_factors.factor: High switching costs on embedded systems
moat_factors.description: Long-tenured application management, infrastructure outsourcing, and core-platform (Finacle banking software) engagements are deeply embedded in client operations; migrating away from an incumbent IT services provider carries significant business disruption risk, supporting multi-year contract renewals

moat_factors.factor: Brand and client trust at enterprise scale
moat_factors.description: Recognized as a Leader across dozens of third-party analyst rankings (Gartner, Everest Group, HFS Horizons, Forrester) in cloud, AI, SAP, banking, and engineering services categories, which supports large-deal win rates ($14.9B TCV in FY2026) with Fortune 500-type clients

Strategic collaborations with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, AWS, NVIDIA, Intel, Cursor, and Cognition position Infosys Topaz as an orchestration layer across leading AI model providers, though differentiation versus peers pursuing similar multi-vendor AI partnerships is not yet clearly proven

The core offshore labor-cost arbitrage that built the Indian IT industry is increasingly commoditized as peers replicate the same model, and is now also structurally challenged by generative AI, which can substitute for some lower-value offshore coding/testing/maintenance labor

weaknesses: Commoditized core service lines (application maintenance, testing, basic BPM) face margin and pricing pressure from GenAI-driven productivity tools that reduce billable hours per unit of client work

Revenue growth has been structurally low (low-single-digit percent in constant currency, FY2026 guidance of just 1.5-3.5%), reflecting a mature, highly competitive industry with limited organic volume growth versus a decade ago

Heavy reliance on US/Europe client discretionary IT budgets, concentrated in large multinational enterprise accounts, with no meaningfully differentiated product moat versus TCS, Accenture, or Cognizant in most service lines
US H-1B visa policy and immigration-related regulatory/legal risk (DOJ investigation into H-1B visa classification practices) creates both cost and reputational overhang unique to this business model
Elevated attrition and wage inflation in the Indian IT labor market historically compress margins faster than pricing can offset, though attrition has normalized from pandemic-era peaks

growth_drivers: AI services expansion — AI-related revenue reached 8.2% of total revenue in Q1 FY2027 and has been growing at double-digit sequential rates for several quarters, driven by the Infosys Topaz Fabric platform spanning AI strategy, data, process transformation, legacy modernization, physical AI, and trust/governance

Large deal wins — TCV of large deals reached $14.9 billion in FY2026 (55% net new) and $3.6 billion in Q1 FY2027 (61% net new), providing multi-year revenue visibility as enterprises consolidate IT spending with fewer, larger strategic partners for AI-led transformation

Cloud migration and modernization (Infosys Cobalt) — continued enterprise migration from legacy infrastructure to hyperscaler cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) remains a multi-year secular tailwind

Strategic AI partnerships with foundation model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, NVIDIA) and agentic coding tool vendors (Cursor, Cognition, Harness) positioning Infosys as an integration/orchestration layer for enterprise AI adoption at scale
Finacle core-banking platform wins (e.g., Bank of Sydney, Sterling Bank of Asia, Producers Bank) extending Infosys's reach in financial services software beyond pure services delivery
Project Maximus cost-efficiency program generating savings that management has redeployed into AI, talent, and sales/marketing investment, supporting margin resilience even amid soft top-line growth
Capital allocation discipline (~85% of 5-year cumulative FCF returned via dividends/buybacks) supporting EPS growth even in a low organic revenue growth environment

business.risk: Generative AI disruption to the core services model
business.description: Industry estimates suggest GenAI could impact 25-30% of traditional application development, testing, and maintenance work, potentially creating a 10-12% revenue headwind over 3-4 years absent offsetting new AI-services revenue; this directly threatens the offshore labor-arbitrage model underpinning Infosys's historical growth and margins

business.risk: Client concentration and discretionary IT spending cyclicality
business.description: Revenue is driven by large enterprise clients' discretionary technology budgets, which can be deferred or cut quickly in a macro slowdown; FY2026/FY2027 guidance of only 1.5-3.5% constant-currency growth reflects a cautious demand environment

Intensifying competition among TCS, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, and Accenture, combined with clients demanding AI-driven productivity gains be passed through as cost savings, pressures per-unit pricing even as volumes hold
LTM voluntary attrition of ~12.6% and the need to continuously reskill ~325,000 employees for AI-era service delivery creates ongoing cost and execution risk

financial.description: Revenue is reported in USD but the large majority of operating costs (employee compensation) are INR-denominated; rupee appreciation compresses margins while depreciation provides a tailwind, and currency volatility makes quarter-to-quarter margin trends harder to interpret for USD-based ADR investors

financial.risk: Capital return policy constrains reinvestment flexibility
financial.description: Commitment to return ~85% of cumulative 5-year FCF via dividends/buybacks leaves less capital for transformative M&A or aggressive AI infrastructure investment relative to some global peers, though this has historically been viewed as a positive capital discipline signal rather than a risk

regulatory.description: A $100,000 fee imposed on certain new H-1B petitions in September 2025 (subsequently vacated by a federal court in mid-2026, pending appeal) directly targets the visa category Infosys relies on for onsite US staffing; Infosys filed over 2,000 H-1B petitions with ~93%+ of new hires potentially affected, and continued legal/political uncertainty over the fee's ultimate status is a persistent overhang

The DOJ is investigating how Infosys classified certain H-1B visa-recipient employees working for a client in immigration filings; the company is in discussions with the DOJ, and any adverse finding could carry financial penalties and reputational damage

regulatory.risk: India labor law and tax regime changes
regulatory.description: India's new Labour Codes (notified November 2025) increased gratuity and leave liabilities by $143 million in FY2026 alone; ongoing Indian corporate tax assessments and disputes (some resolved favorably via tax order reversals in FY2026) add earnings volatility

regulatory.risk: Data privacy and cross-border data regulation
regulatory.description: Expanding data localization and privacy regulations (GDPR enforcement, emerging US state privacy laws, India's DPDP Act) raise compliance costs across the global client base Infosys serves

macro.risk: US and European IT spending cycles
macro.description: Over 88% of FY2026 revenue came from North America and Europe combined; a recession or sustained enterprise IT budget freeze in either region would directly compress Infosys's growth, as seen in the sub-5% growth environment of FY2024-FY2027

Management explicitly flagged 'the effect of current and any future tariffs' as a forward-looking risk factor, reflecting broader uncertainty in US trade policy that could indirectly affect client capex/opex decisions

Rising nationalism/protectionism in major markets (visa restrictions, data localization, 'reshoring' rhetoric) could structurally disadvantage the offshore-delivery model that Indian IT services firms depend on

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global IT services market projected to grow from ~$1.6 trillion (2025) to ~$3.48 trillion by 2034 (CAGR ~8.9%), driven by cloud adoption, digital transformation, and rising enterprise AI spending; however, near-term growth for traditional offshore-heavy players like Infosys has slowed to low-single-digits as GenAI reshapes demand away from legacy application maintenance toward AI consulting/implementation, and as macro uncertainty causes enterprise clients to delay large discretionary projects
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate to high - IT services demand is tied to corporate capex/opex cycles and tends to lag the broader economy by 1-2 quarters on both the way down and the recovery; large multi-year outsourcing deals provide some revenue stability, but discretionary project work (consulting, new development) is highly cyclical
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct sensitivity (no meaningful debt-funded business model) but moderate indirect sensitivity via client capex decisions, M&A activity (which drives consulting/integration work), and the opportunity cost of IT investment versus other capital uses during high-rate periods
key_input_costs: Skilled IT labor compensation (India and onsite US/Europe wages)
US visa fees and immigration compliance costs (H-1B)
Technology/AI infrastructure and cloud computing costs

recent_developments.event: Reported $5,082 million Q1 revenue (2.4% YoY growth in constant currency), operating margin of 21.1%; AI revenues reached 8.2% of total revenue; large deal TCV of $3.6 billion with 61% net new; FY2027 revenue guidance revised down to 1.5-3.0% constant currency growth (from prior 1.5-3.5%), while operating margin guidance of 20-22% was retained; board appointed Ashiss Kumar Dash as CEO-Designate, succeeding Salil Parekh effective April 1, 2027, with a structured transition beginning October 1, 2026

FY2026 revenue crossed $20 billion for the first time ($20,158 million, +3.1% YoY constant currency); reported operating margin 20.3% (adjusted non-IFRS 21.0%, excluding $143 million one-time impact from India's new Labour Codes); FY2026 large deal TCV of $14.9 billion (55% net new); FY2027 initial guidance set at 1.5-3.5% revenue growth and 20-22% operating margin; board proposed final dividend of ₹25/share, bringing total FY2026 shareholder returns (dividends + buyback) to over ₹37,500 crore

Completed ₹18,000 crore share buyback (approved by shareholders November 6, 2025) at ₹1,800 per share, repurchasing ~1% of outstanding shares, as part of the capital allocation policy targeting ~85% cumulative 5-year free cash flow returned to shareholders

US H-1B visa fee of $100,000 for certain new petitions (effective September 21, 2025) created near-term cost and hiring-strategy uncertainty for Infosys's US onsite staffing model; a federal court vacated the fee in mid-2026 and an appeals court denied government efforts to reinstate it, but legal uncertainty persists pending further appeal

US Department of Justice continuing its investigation into Infosys's classification of H-1B visa employees working at a client site in immigration filings; company remains in discussions with the DOJ with no resolution disclosed as of the Q1 FY2027 filing

Headcount declined by 8,440 employees quarter-over-quarter to 328,594 (though up year-over-year from 323,578 in March 2025); voluntary attrition (LTM) rose to 12.6%; utilization (ex-trainees) remained elevated at ~83%, signaling tighter workforce management amid still-soft demand

Expanded AI partnership ecosystem with major announcements involving OpenAI (Codex), Anthropic (Claude Code), NVIDIA, Intel, Cursor, Cognition (Devin), and Harness, positioning Infosys Topaz Fabric as a multi-vendor AI orchestration and agentic engineering platform for enterprise clients

items.notes: Narrowed/lowered from the initial FY2027 guidance of 1.5-3.5% given at Q4 FY2026 results (April 2026), reflecting a more cautious demand environment despite record large deal TCV
Unchanged from initial FY2027 guidance; management emphasizes 'resilient' margins (21.1% in Q1 FY2027) driven by Project Maximus cost savings offsetting wage/AI investment costs

items.target: no explicit numeric target, but management highlights continued strong bookings momentum
items.notes: $3.6 billion TCV in Q1 FY2027 with 61% net new (up from 55% net new for full FY2026's $14.9 billion), cited as evidence of market share gains in large transformation deals

items.target: no explicit percentage target, described as accelerating
items.notes: AI revenue reached 8.2% of total revenue in Q1 FY2027, with management citing 'double-digit quarter-on-quarter' AI revenue growth for several consecutive quarters

items.target: ~85% of cumulative 5-year FCF returned via dividends and buybacks
items.notes: FY2026 FCF was $3.73 billion (112.6% of net profit); ~82.1% of cumulative FY2025-FY2026 FCF already returned to shareholders via dividends and the ₹18,000 crore buyback

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Salil Parekh emphasized that 'AI momentum is now rapidly converting into revenue,' citing Infosys Topaz-powered large deal wins as evidence of market share gains and positioning Infosys as 'the strategic partner of choice for AI transformation.' CFO Jayesh Sanghrajka described margins as 'resilient' amid 'a challenging business environment,' noting the company is 'accelerating investments in AI, talent, and platforms to drive future growth' while maintaining 'the financial flexibility needed to capitalize on emerging opportunities.' The lowered FY2027 revenue guidance (vs. the April 2026 initial range) signals incremental caution about near-term demand even as large-deal bookings and AI-related revenue both show strong momentum.

bull_case: Market share gains in large transformation deals — record $14.9 billion FY2026 and $3.6 billion Q1 FY2027 large-deal TCV with rising net-new mix (61%) suggest Infosys is winning share even in a soft-growth industry environment

AI services are an emerging, fast-growing revenue stream (8.2% of revenue, growing double-digit sequentially) that could offset GenAI's disruptive impact on legacy application/maintenance work if Infosys successfully repositions as an AI implementation partner rather than a pure labor-arbitrage vendor

Resilient margins (20-22% guided, consistently delivered) and strong free cash flow generation (FCF conversion often exceeding 100% of net profit) support a disciplined, shareholder-friendly capital return policy (~85% of 5-year cumulative FCF) even in a low-growth revenue environment

Smooth, long-planned CEO succession (Ashiss Kumar Dash, a 31-year Infosys veteran, named CEO-designate with a structured transition through March 2027) reduces leadership continuity risk relative to peers facing abrupt transitions

Diversified industry vertical exposure (financial services, manufacturing, retail, life sciences) and broad AI ecosystem partnerships (OpenAI, Anthropic, NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft) reduce single-partner or single-vertical dependency risk
bear_case: Generative AI poses a structural, not cyclical, threat to the core offshore labor-arbitrage services model — estimates suggest 25-30% of traditional application development/testing/maintenance work could be disrupted, with a potential 10-12% revenue headwind over 3-4 years that AI-services revenue growth may not fully offset

Revenue growth has stagnated at low-single-digit constant-currency rates for multiple consecutive years (FY2027 guidance just 1.5-3.0%, already lowered once this fiscal year), reflecting a mature, intensely competitive industry with limited organic volume growth

US H-1B visa policy risk remains unresolved — the $100,000 fee was vacated by courts but remains under appeal, and the unrelated DOJ investigation into H-1B visa classification practices creates both financial and reputational overhang specific to Infosys's US onsite staffing model

Heavy geographic concentration (~88% of revenue from North America and Europe combined) leaves Infosys fully exposed to any US/European enterprise IT spending slowdown or recession, with limited diversification into faster-growing emerging markets

No clear structural moat versus TCS, Accenture, Cognizant, Wipro, or HCLTech in most service lines — competitive differentiation rests largely on execution and relationships rather than durable technology or network-effect advantages, making sustained premium growth or margin expansion difficult to defend
